notes:
## Effects of sleep deprivation on cognitive performance
The effects of sleep deprivation on cognitive performance are a broad range of impairments resulting from inadequate sleep, impacting attention, executive function and memory. Recent 2025 research specifies these include reduced cognitive flexibility (task-switching accuracy after total sleep deprivation) and prolonged auditory P300 latency with slower reaction time in healthy adults. An estimated 20% of adults or more have some form of sleep deprivation. It may come with insomnia or major depressive disorder, or indicate other mental disorders. The consequences can negatively affect the health, cognition, energy level and mood of a person and anyone around. It increases the risk of human error, especially with technology.

## Sleep deprivation
Sleep deprivation, also known as sleep insufficiency or sleeplessness, is the health condition of not having adequate duration or quality of sleep to support proper alertness, performance, and health. It can be either chronic or acute and may vary widely in severity. This means it can occur over both short and long periods. Sleep is important because adequate sleep, or restful sleep, is essential for maintaining overall health, brain performance, emotional regulation, and metabolic balance. Persistent sleep insufficiency can contribute to cognitive decline, emotional instability, and biological wear that has effects similar to accelerated aging. Scientific research demonstrates that inadequate sleep produces chronic consequences for overall health, ranging from attentional lapses to long-term neurodegenerative changes.
The human body and most living organisms depend on sleep for neural recovery. All known animals sleep or exhibit some form of sleep behavior, and the importance of sleep is self-evident for humans, as nearly a third of a person's life is spent sleeping. Sleep deprivation is common, affecting about one-third of the population.
The US National Sleep Foundation recommends...

## Sleep hygiene
Sleep hygiene is a behavioral and environmental practice developed in the late 1970s as a method to help people with mild to moderate insomnia. Clinicians assess the sleep hygiene of people with insomnia and other conditions, such as depression, and offer recommendations based on the assessment.
Sleep hygiene recommendations include establishing a regular sleep schedule, taking no or short naps, not exercising physically (or mentally) too close to bedtime, limiting worry, limiting exposure to light in the hours before sleep, and getting out of bed if sleep does not come. Additionally, use of the bed for anything but sleep and sex, avoiding alcohol (as well as nicotine, caffeine, and other stimulants) in the hours before bedtime, and having a peaceful, comfortable and dark sleep environment, are other hygiene recommendations.

## Hygiene
Hygiene is a set of practices performed to preserve health.
According to the World Health Organization (WHO), "Hygiene refers to conditions and practices that help to maintain health and prevent the spread of diseases." Personal hygiene refers to maintaining the body's cleanliness. Hygiene activities can be grouped into the following: home and everyday hygiene, personal hygiene, medical hygiene, sleep hygiene, and food hygiene. Home and every day hygiene includes hand washing, respiratory hygiene, food hygiene at home, hygiene in the kitchen, hygiene in the bathroom, laundry hygiene, and medical hygiene at home.
While often equated with cleanliness in common usage, hygiene is a term encompassing the personal practices and environmental conditions that maintain health and prevent disease.

plan.title: How Sleep Shapes Memory, and How to Sleep Better
plan.description: Sleep deprivation harms attention, executive function and memory, and it affects about one-third of people. This video explains what a lack of sleep does to thinking and which sleep hygiene habits can help.

beats.narration: You studied hard all evening, then stayed up late to keep going. The next morning, the facts feel slippery. What happened to them? The answer may be in the hours you skipped.

props.title: Sleep and Memory
props.subtitle: What a lack of sleep does to your mind, and how to fix it

beats.narration: Nearly a third of your life is spent asleep. That is a huge investment. Every known animal sleeps or shows some form of sleep behavior, which hints that it does something essential.

props.label: of a person's life is spent sleeping

beats.narration: Adequate, restful sleep supports four things: overall health, brain performance, emotional regulation, and metabolic balance. Your body and brain use that time for neural recovery, like a nightly repair shift.

So what happens when sleep falls short? Sleep deprivation means not having enough duration or quality of sleep to support proper alertness, performance and health. It can be short-term or chronic, and mild or severe.

props.definition: Not having adequate duration or quality of sleep to support proper alertness, performance, and health.

beats.narration: It is far more common than you might think. About one-third of the population is affected, and one estimate says twenty percent of adults or more have some form of sleep deprivation.

props.label: About one-third of people are affected
props.title: Sleep deprivation is common

beats.chapter: What lack of sleep does to thinking

beats.narration: The effects are broad. Poor sleep impairs three big areas of thinking: attention, executive function, which is your ability to plan and manage tasks, and memory. That is why yesterday's study session can vanish.

Recent research adds detail. After total sleep deprivation, healthy adults showed reduced cognitive flexibility, meaning less accurate task-switching. Their brain responses were also slower, with longer auditory P300 latency and slower reaction times.

props.heading: Findings in healthy adults
items: P300 latency: brain response is prolonged

beats.narration: The damage goes beyond a bad day. Persistent sleep loss can contribute to cognitive decline, emotional instability, and biological wear similar to accelerated aging. It also raises the risk of human error, especially with technology.
The good news is that sleep habits can be trained. Since the late 1970s, clinicians have used a set of practices called sleep hygiene to help people with mild to moderate insomnia.

props.definition: Behavioral and environmental practices developed in the late 1970s to help people with mild to moderate insomnia.

beats.narration: Start with timing. Keep a regular sleep schedule. Take no naps, or only short ones. And do not exercise physically, or mentally, too close to bedtime, because your body needs time to wind down.

Next, calm your evening. Limit worry. Limit exposure to light in the hours before sleep. And avoid alcohol, nicotine, caffeine and other stimulants in the hours before bed, since they work against rest.
Then shape the room. A peaceful, comfortable and dark sleep environment helps. Use your bed for sleep, and sex, only. That teaches your brain that bed means rest, not scrolling or working.
And if sleep does not come, get out of bed. Lying there frustrated links your bed with wakefulness. Do something quiet elsewhere, then return when you feel sleepy.

nodes.label: Get out of bed, stay calm

beats.narration: So here is the one idea to keep. Sleep is when your brain recovers, and your memory depends on it. Protect your nights with regular, dark, calm habits, and tomorrow's mind will thank you.

props.text: Protect your sleep, and you protect your memory.
